title: Stop That Pawn!
reviewNotes: Three branches compare supported seven-piece diagrams after Kxf3 at 94s and Qb8/Kd1 at 50s. Source b8=Q/h1=Q/Qb7+ diagonal skewer wins, while an independently supplied Ke2 flight confirms the first-rank skewer with Kd1. Copying Qb1 when the king instead stands on f3 loses the queen. Earlier larger knight/bishop sacrifices remain source context.
transcript: The genius of white plays knight to d2, [music] a beautiful sacrifice, realizing that promoting to a queen wouldn't be enough. After h takes g1 queen, this would be a drawn end game. But what even is the point of this sacrifice? Well, of course now black cannot promote to a queen because this would allow a fork of the king and queen with the knight, and white would collect the queen [music] and win the game. So black has to accept the sacrifice really and take the knight. And it seems like nothing has been achieved. It's not like the bishop can defend against [music] because the black pawn would be able to capture it. But white finds another majestic idea. The brilliant bishop to d1 [music] check, sacrificing the last one of his pieces. But this time the sacrifice cannot be accepted. If the king does take the bishop, now white can promote [music] to a queen, and after black does the same, there is going to be a check and a skewer that would pick up the black queen. But [music] okay, so what? The king doesn't have to take that bishop. It can simply move to f2, make sure that the bishop can again not stop the pawn from promoting, and all is going to go well, right? Well, not exactly, because there is no worse feeling than thinking you stopped a move and then seeing your opponent playing it anyway. Bishop to f3 is a incredible idea because of course the bishop has to be captured. If you don't, it can forever live on this diagonal, prevent the promotion of the pawn, and then white would get a queen. So black really has no other choice but to take the bishop. But now finally, with only one pawn left, white promotes, black does the same, and we have aligned up the black king and the black queen perfectly to deliver another skewer on b7. White is going to collect the black queen and win this [music] beautiful end game.
